clauses.section: 3.11 How apparent ambiguities are resolved
clauses.text: - **R1 dangling else.** `else` only follows a `Block` (statement `if`) or is mandatory (`if … then … else …` expression). A statement `if` ends at its `DEDENT`, so the next `else` at the same indentation belongs to it.

clauses.section: 3.11 How apparent ambiguities are resolved
clauses.text: - **R2 `try … else` against `if … then … else`.** The branches of an `if` expression and the operands of `try` are `CatchExpr`, which cannot contain a bare `try` or `if`. `if c then try a else b` is a syntax error; write `if c then (try a else b) else d`.

clauses.section: 3.11 How apparent ambiguities are resolved
clauses.text: - **R3 comparison chains.** `0 < a < 10` is a syntax error (non-associative). Write `a in 0..10`.

clauses.section: 3.11 How apparent ambiguities are resolved
clauses.text: - **R4 assignment against equality.** `=` is a statement form, never an expression; `(x = 1)` is a syntax error.

clauses.section: 3.11 How apparent ambiguities are resolved
clauses.text: - **R5 generic call against index.** `f[T](x)` parses as `index(f, T)` then a call; name resolution (4.3) turns an index of a generic function or type by type arguments into instantiation, as in Go.

clauses.section: 3.11 How apparent ambiguities are resolved
clauses.text: - **R6 impl generics against slice types.** `impl [T] …` would be ambiguous with the slice type `[T]`, so impl parameters need `forall`: `impl forall[T: Show] Show for List[T]`.

clauses.section: 3.11 How apparent ambiguities are resolved
clauses.text: - **R7 labels.** In argument and pattern lists `NAME ":"` is always a label. Map literals `{k: v}` are in a different bracket, so `{a: 1}` is a map whose key is the variable `a` (write `{"a": 1}` for a text key).

clauses.section: 3.11 How apparent ambiguities are resolved
clauses.text: - **R8 variant patterns against bindings.** A `Path` pattern is a unit variant if name resolution finds a variant of that name in scope, otherwise it binds a fresh variable (Rust's rule). W-PAT-1 reports that a binding which shadows a variant name requires change, so a misspelled variant is never silently a binding.

clauses.section: 3.11 How apparent ambiguities are resolved
clauses.text: - **R9 send.** `<-` after an expression at statement level is a send; in prefix position it is a receive. The two never meet: `a <- <- b` is "send the value received from b to a".

clauses.section: 3.11 How apparent ambiguities are resolved
clauses.text: - **R10 the words of a law.** `always`, `every` and `attest` are words of the grammar only at the start of a line inside a `law` block, and `applied` and a `kept` with no `:` only as the whole outcome of an `every step` line; everywhere else each is a NAME, so no identifier is reserved for them. A bool field named `applied` is read in that outcome as `(applied)`. `law` itself is reserved (2.4).

clauses.text: A borrow cannot be stored in a field, a collection, a channel message, an event, a state, a closure that escapes, or be returned: with one exception: a function whose return type is a borrow (`-> &[T]`) must return a borrow derived from a parameter, and the result is tied to that parameter (R-RET).

clauses.text: - `chan[τ](n)` creates a channel with capacity n (a comptime or runtime usize; 0 means rendezvous) and type `chan τ`; τ must be a data type or a `chan`.

clauses.section: 5.9 Traits

clauses.section: 6.2 Evaluation
clauses.text: - **E1 Fuel exhaustion is uncatchable.** Running out of fuel is not a declared error and not a trap a program can observe: no `catch`, `try` or `try e else X` handles it, it propagates outward through every construct, and it keeps the state exactly as a trap does (T8). The derivation: if a handler could observe exhaustion, a program could return a different value on a larger budget, and a completed result would depend on fuel. The fuel laws require that it does not: more fuel never changes a completed result (`RCE.Core.eval_mono`, `eval_fuel_indep` in `lean/RCE/Core/Fuel.lean`). A conforming r

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **N1 Numbers.** A Form number is an int (i64, or u64 per N2) or a float (finite f64). The type is part of the value and is kept across every boundary: a float with no fractional part stays a float (`10.0` is written `10.0` in canonical JSON, `10` is an int), and `-0.0` keeps its sign (N3 F6). Derivation: encoding must be injective and round-trip, `decode(encode(v)) == v`, because replay rebuilds state from D. Turning `10.0` into `10` at a boundary would decode as an int, changing the static type a later step sees and the bits of later float arithmetic, so no normalization is applied. RCE's s

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **N2 Integer arithmetic** is checked: overflow of the *static type's* range is `trap("overflow: V is outside T")` with V the exact result and T the static type (`i64` for an untyped literal), never a wrap. `/` truncates toward zero (`-7 / 2 = -3`); `%` has the sign of the dividend (`-3 % 2 = -1`). Division or remainder by zero is `trap("division by zero")`. Modular and clamped arithmetic are explicit methods, never the default: `a.wrapping_add(b)`, `wrapping_sub`, `wrapping_mul` give the result modulo 2^N mapped into the static type's range, and `saturating_add`, `saturating_sub`, `saturatin

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **N3 Floats.** The rules below are derived from IEEE 754-2019 and from two requirements of the Form: replay must give the same bits on every target (T1), and δ must be total (S1). `tests/float_rules.rs` checks each rule on the interpreter; the parity set carries the vectors of `examples/57_float_vectors.rce` to every CI target.

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **F1 Correct rounding.** f64 is IEEE binary64. `+ - * /` and `sqrt` are the standard's basic operations, correctly rounded with roundTiesToEven, the default rounding-direction attribute; so are the conversion of an integer (`as f64`) and of a decimal literal. A correctly rounded operation is a function of its operands' bits alone, so every conforming target gives the same result: this is the only property determinism needs, and no other rounding mode exists in RCE.

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **F2 One rounding per operator, in source order.** Float addition and multiplication are not associative and `a * b + c` with one rounding differs from two roundings (vector `MulSub`: `0.1 * 10.0 - 1.0` is `0`, fused it is `5.551115123125783e-17`). Contraction to fused multiply-add, reassociation, excess precision and every other value-changing optimization the standard allows a language to permit are therefore not valid compilations (HC-14). A fused multiply-add is itself correctly rounded, so it may exist only as an explicit named operation; RCE has none yet. Adding one needs a correctly r

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **F3 Subnormals are preserved.** Gradual underflow is part of the binary64 format; flush-to-zero and denormals-are-zero modes are not IEEE operations and would make `x - y == 0` hold for `x != y`. A host never enables them (HC-13); vectors `Mul(5e-324, 3.0)` and `Mul(2.2250738585072014e-308, 0.5)` detect either mode.

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **F4 Non-finite results trap (from totality).** A Form value must have a reflexive equality and a total order (6.2, N5, N6) and must encode as a JSON number for hashing (N1). NaN is unequal to itself under IEEE comparison, and an infinity is not a JSON number and reintroduces NaN through `inf - inf` and `0 * inf`; the largest subset of binary64 closed under these requirements is the finite values. δ is total as a function into values and traps, so an operation whose IEEE result is not finite (the standard's overflow, divideByZero and invalid exceptions) is `trap("non-finite float")`. The alt

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **F5 NaN payloads are never observable.** By F4 no NaN becomes a value, so its sign, payload and quiet bit cannot reach state, output or a hash; the standard leaves payload propagation to the implementation, which is why this matters. An implementation tests for a non-finite result before any NaN escapes, and the trap text is the same for every NaN. A fabric or target that can produce NaN (GPU, NPU, WASM SIMD) canonicalizes or traps before a value reaches state (HC-13; `wasm_float.rs` rewrites NaN to the canonical positive NaN).

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **F6 Signed zero is a distinct state.** `-0.0` arises by the standard's sign rules, which are exact, so every target produces it in the same places (vector `Mul(0.0, -1.0)`). It is observable: `tostr` prints `-0` (f64 and f32 alike, so text round-trips), and the sign decides later results through the same exact rules. The state hash must be injective on observable state, so canonical JSON keeps the sign and a state holding `-0.0` hashes differently from one holding `0.0`; the canonical order (6.1) is totalOrder, so they are distinct map keys. `-0.0 == 0.0` is still true: `==` is IEEE compari

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **F7 Exception flags are not state.** Inexact and underflow raise nothing (F1 already fixes the result); overflow, divideByZero and invalid are the trap of F4. No program reads a flag.

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **F8 Exact operations.** `floor`, `ceil` and `round` are the standard's roundToIntegral operations toward negative, toward positive and ties-away (`(2.5).round()` is `3`, `(-2.5).round()` is `-3`); `abs` clears the sign. `min` and `max` follow N5. None of these rounds.

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **F9 Transcendentals are correctly rounded RCE code, or absent.** IEEE 754-2019 recommends but does not require correctly rounded `exp`, `log`, `sin`, `pow` and the like, and platform math libraries differ in the last bit, so no runtime takes one from its platform library and no Form op names one. A transcendental exists only as RCE source in the standard library module `math` (`stdlib/lib/math/math.rce`), built from the operations of F1 to F8 and integers, so every runtime carries the same algorithm and the result is the same bits on every target (vector parity: Rust, Python, JavaScript, Sc

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **N4 Mixed arithmetic** does not exist in RCE (both operands of a binary operator have the same static type). `a as f64` converts an integer exactly when |a| ≤ 2^53 and otherwise rounds to nearest even; `x as iN` truncates toward zero and traps if the result is out of range or x is not finite.

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **N5 min / max** compare exactly on integers and by IEEE order on floats (total, since operands are finite); on a tie the receiver is returned.

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **N6 Equality** is structural value equality within one static type; `1 == 1.0` is a type error (the type is part of the value, N1). Float `==` is IEEE comparison, so `-0.0 == 0.0` although the two are distinct states (N3 F6).

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **N7 Text** is a sequence of Unicode scalar values compared by code point, stored as UTF-8. From draft 0.5, `len`, indexing and slicing count UTF-8 bytes (Form `blen`, `bget`, `bslice`): `s[i]` is a `u8`, and a slice whose ends are not character boundaries is `trap("not a char boundary")`. `for c in s` and `chars()` still go by character. Case mapping (`upper`, `lower`) and class tests (`isdigit`, `isalpha`, `isupper`, `islower`) are ASCII-only; other characters are unchanged / false. `strip`, `words` and `toint` treat as whitespace exactly the 25 code points of the White_Space property of U

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **N8 Indexing** The index `i` of `a[i]` and the ends of `a[i:j]` have type `usize` (W-TY-1 otherwise), so no index is negative. `a[i]` with i ≥ n is `trap("index i out of range")`. A slice end above n is `trap("slice index out of range")`, and i > j is `trap("slice bounds reversed")`; an omitted end is 0 or n. Indexing and slicing are total or trapping by one rule: an out-of-range position is never silently moved.

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **N9 Limits.** A list or text built by any operation is at most SIZE_LIMIT = 1,000,000 elements (`trap("size limit")`). A value written to state is at most VALUE_LIMIT = 1,048,576 bytes of canonical JSON (`trap("value limit")`, the state is kept, the value is not recorded).

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **N10 Absence.** `none` and a present `()` differ, exactly as the Form's null-versus-absent rule: an option field holding none is present.

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **N11 Time** is the logical clock only: `Tick` events and `after n` in `select`. No construct reads a wall clock.

clauses.text: - W-MOD-3 An import's name (`q` of `use p.q`, `r` of `use p.q as r`) that clashes with a declaration of the importing module or names two different modules. The items of an imported module are reached only through that name (4.1), so an item never clashes with the importer's items or with another module's, `pub` or not; `use p.q as r` resolves a clash.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what requires change at entry
clauses.text: - W-SAFE-1 The identifiers `unsafe`, `Rc`, `Arc`, `RefCell`, `transmute`, `static`: requires change, with "memory safety is by construction" (there are no escape hatches in RCE other than the `extern` boundary of 5.11).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what requires change at entry

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what requires change at entry

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what requires change at entry
clauses.text: - W-STEP-1 A `step` naming an undeclared region or matching an undeclared event. W-STEP-2 **Totality**: an event that no step and no actor handler can ever match. W-STEP-3 The arrow form on a region with more than one field. W-STEP-4 Within one region, two unguarded steps whose patterns overlap (the second is unreachable).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what requires change at entry
clauses.text: - W-EFF-1 `emit`, `spawn`, channel operations or `select` in a pure `fn`; reading another region's fields in a step; calling a foreign function anywhere but `fn main` or a task function.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what requires change at entry
clauses.text: - W-REC-1 A cycle in the call graph, including through trait methods after monomorphization, other than a cycle of plain functions (one function calling itself included) whose calls are done by layered summed measures, or each of whose cycles of calls passes through a function declared with `bound` (6.7); `par` or `for … par` in a function of a cycle with a bounded function; `bound` on an iterator, a foreign function or a trait signature.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what requires change at entry
clauses.text: - W-CT-1 Comptime code that calls a non-comptime-safe function or traps or exceeds fuel.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what requires change at entry
clauses.text: - W-INT-1 An `example` or `check` that does not hold.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what requires change at entry
clauses.text: - W-INT-2 (recommended; never requires change) A module with a step and `example` lines, whose obligations its lookup-table control meets (6.9): `rce check` admits it and prints the recommendation (10.2).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what requires change at entry
clauses.text: - W-LAW-1 A law (6.11) that fails, or that is undecided and not attested (its alphabet is incomplete or the bound LAW_FUEL is reached), or an `attest` line that is not `WHO;YYYY-MM-DD;COVER`. The report of a failing law ends with its counterexample as an `example` line. The trait laws of F.6.6 fall under the same rule once they are implemented.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what requires change at entry
clauses.text: - W-UI-1 A module that emits frames (Appendix E, HC-29) whose frames do not meet `ui.rules`: the frames each `example`'s run derives, judged as one trace, leave a success criterion of WCAG 2.2 level A or AA failing or undecided, or they cannot be judged (no example derives a frame, an emitted `Frame` is not a frame, or judging them exceeds the fuel bound). No `example` or `check` line names `ui.rules`; each finding is one report that names its criterion (E.4f).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what requires change at entry
clauses.text: - W-SIMD-1 A lane-wise operator on arrays of different lengths, of an unfixed length, or with non-numeric lanes (5.1).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what requires change at entry
clauses.text: - W-GRAPH-1 A `tensor` operation or a lane-wise operator inside a graph term on operands of shapes it does not take: a matrix product whose inner lengths differ, an operand of the wrong rank, two tensors of different shapes or of shapes that do not broadcast, an attention whose keys and queries differ in width or whose heads do not divide, a reshape that changes the element count, an axis beyond the rank, a list that is not a permutation of the axes, a block format whose length is not a multiple of 32 (6.13, GT-4).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what requires change at entry
clauses.text: - W-GRAPH-2 An operand of a graph term that is not a tensor of `f32`, `f64`, `i8` or `i32` with every length at least 1, operands of two element types, an operation of floats on integers, ids that are not `i32`, a quantized product whose operands are not `f32`, `i8` and `f32`, a name `std.tensor` does not define, the wrong number of operands, a labelled operand, an axis, epsilon, shape or permutation that is not a literal of its kind, or a `tensor.within` bound that is not an integer literal from 1 to 2^31 − 1 (6.13, GT-1 to GT-4).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what requires change at entry
clauses.text: - W-GRAPH-3 An operation whose level is weaker than the level in force where it stands, that is, a level the program does not declare: a `tensor.round_bf16`, `tensor.round_q8_0` or `tensor.round_q4_0` outside a `tensor.lossy` (6.13, GT-3).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what requires change at entry
clauses.text: - W-LIN-1 A linear value not consumed exactly once on every path, copied, moved inside a loop, or placed in a collection, field, payload, channel or iterator (5.12).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what requires change at entry

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what requires change at entry
clauses.text: - W-ITER-1 An iterator function that is not pure or has an arrow body; `yield` outside an iterator function; an `iter τ` value used other than as a `for` operand or `.collect()` receiver (5.14).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what requires change at entry
clauses.text: - W-REF-1 A refined type (5.1) that is generic, refines a type other than an integer type, `text` or a collection, or whose predicate is outside the decidable fragment (a term other than `self`, `self.len()` or an integer literal, an operator other than a comparison, `and`, `or`, `not`, or a call other than a text character class).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what requires change at entry
clauses.text: - W-LOOP-1 A `LOOP_LIMIT` declaration that is not `const LOOP_LIMIT: u64 = n` with a positive literal n (6.7).

clauses.section: E.2 Admission, time and authority (HC-1 to HC-9)
clauses.text: - **HC-1 One admitter per term.** At any log height a program instance has exactly one admitter, the holder of the current term (E.2b). Every input reaches δ only after the admitter appended it to D, in D's order. The admitter is a role, not a machine: when it fails, another host takes the role for a higher term and continues the same D (E.2b). A host without replication holds term 0 for its lifetime, which is the single admitter of earlier versions.

clauses.section: E.2 Admission, time and authority (HC-1 to HC-9)
clauses.text: - **HC-2 Only the admitter reads clocks.** Wall time and monotonic time enter only as events (`Tick(n)`, `host.WallTime` when an adapter supplies it, and the result of a `WallClock` request, HC-32). Time inside the language is logical (6.3 N11, C.11.12).

clauses.section: E.2 Admission, time and authority (HC-1 to HC-9)
clauses.text: - **HC-3 Typed output requests.** Each effect requested by λ (a write, a send, a draw, a foreign call) has exactly one result event: delivered, failed, timed out or unreachable. A result is delivered as the module declares its event, and a result the module declares no event for is recorded in D (E.4c, HD-1). A race inside the adapter (for example a file checked and then opened) is resolved by the adapter; the program sees one atomic outcome. The answer of a model runtime (F.5.6) is delivered only on an event the program declares `extern "model" event`, and the host fills no capability for it

clauses.section: E.2 Admission, time and authority (HC-1 to HC-9)
clauses.text: - **HC-4 Foreign code.** Foreign code runs only through 5.11, with its arguments copied or borrowed for the call only, under fuel, and its result or trap logged as `Foreign(f, arguments, result)`. An isolated component boundary (a WebAssembly component per call) is the recommended adapter; it does not change the rule.

clauses.section: E.2 Admission, time and authority (HC-1 to HC-9)
clauses.text: - **HC-5 Capabilities.** Authority comes only from capabilities minted by logged events (5.16 `Cap[A]` in a version 0.8 module). The host holds no ambient authority on the program's behalf. This is the sandbox, and its contract is independent of any OS: the checker admits only programs whose effects go through granted capabilities, and the deterministic host does not perform any effect without one, before any OS layer is involved. clauses.text: - **HC-5a The printed target is the installed target.** The line a host prints when it enters an OS target is generated from the rules it installed, so it names each restriction at the granularity the target enforces and never one the target did not install. The reference (`sandbox.rs`) lists every address an adapter may use with how it is used: connected to (`net`, `peer`), bound after the target is entered (`net`, and a `http` address whose bind is still being retried), or bound before (`http`, `chan`), whose listener is then only accepted on. clauses.text: - **HC-6 Tick scheduler.** Concurrency runs under the tick semantics of 6.8. clauses.section: E.2 Admission, time and authority (HC-1 to HC-9)
clauses.text: - **HC-7 Numerics and limits.** The host reproduces 6.3 bit for bit and enforces fuel, SIZE_LIMIT and VALUE_LIMIT (6.7, N9) as the reference does, on every run.

clauses.section: E.2 Admission, time and authority (HC-1 to HC-9)
clauses.text: - **HC-7a Fuel per input.** A host is event driven, so fuel is charged per admitted input: each input (one application of δ, including constructing its event) starts with the full fuel of 6.7, and no budget is shared across inputs. Every input has its own bound and a session never starves however long it runs. The reference trace (`rce trace`), the host and replay all reset fuel per input, so a kept step for fuel is a function of that input and the state before it, and D is the same on each.

clauses.section: E.2 Admission, time and authority (HC-1 to HC-9)
clauses.text: - **HC-8 Replay.** A host offers a replay mode that reads D, disconnects every adapter and re-derives every state hash. Replay reads no clock, file, network, device or environment (T37).

clauses.section: E.2 Admission, time and authority (HC-1 to HC-9)
clauses.text: - **HC-9 Priority admission.** Interrupt sources carry a priority in 0..255 (T25, C.11.12). Inputs admitted together are ordered by priority, highest first. Inputs with a source and sequence number are ordered by the window key of HC-15. Inputs given together without source identity (`admit_simultaneous`) are ordered by priority, then by the bytes of their canonical event JSON, so the order is a function of the set of inputs and not of the order the caller passed them in. clauses.section: E.2a Canonical admission (HC-15 to HC-17)
clauses.text: The order of D must not depend on when inputs arrive.

clauses.section: E.2a Canonical admission (HC-15 to HC-17)
clauses.text: - **HC-15 Windows.** Every input carries its source id (text), a per-source sequence number (1, 2, ... with no reuse) and the logical tick its source stamped on it. When the module declares `event Tick(n: u64)`, a window closes when a `Tick(n)` input not yet in D is offered: window k gets `upto = n`, holds every offered input with tick at most `upto` that is not already in D, and the `Tick(n)` is its last input. The boundary is therefore a logged fact, never a wall clock and never a choice of the caller. An input whose tick is at or below the `upto` of the last window in D is late: it is admit

clauses.section: E.2a Canonical admission (HC-15 to HC-17)
clauses.text: - **HC-16 Exactly once.** The dedupe key is (source, seq). A (source, seq) already in D, or offered twice, is a duplicate and is not appended again. Two copies of one (source, seq) with different payloads are ordered by their event bytes, and the lower one is admitted, so the choice does not depend on arrival. An input after a gap in its source's sequence is held for a later window, so each source is admitted in its own order and nothing is skipped. A source retransmits until acked, and the admitter acks an input only after the barrier (HS-2) that covers its window succeeded. A crash before th

clauses.section: E.2a Canonical admission (HC-15 to HC-17)
clauses.text: - **HC-17 Window entries.** Closing a window appends `host.Window` {count, id, term, upto}, then, before each admitted input, `host.Input` {late (only when true), seq, source, window}. The dedupe state is the fold of these entries: on open and on replay the admitter rebuilds, per source, the highest seq in D. A `host.Input` counts only when the program entry it announces follows it, so a cut between the two (HS-4) admits nothing. These are host entries: δ never reads them and they leave the state hash unchanged.

clauses.section: E.2b Replicated D and admitter failover (HC-18 to HC-20)
clauses.text: - **HC-18 Interface.** A replicated log offers the host the Store of E.3 with two additions: `elect(term)`, which succeeds only with grants from a quorum of replicas, each of which then promises not to accept an append from a lower term, and returns the most up-to-date log among the granting quorum, ordered by (term of the last write, length); and an append at a term that a replica accepts only while it has promised no higher term. The barrier succeeds only when a quorum accepted every entry up to it, so a durable entry (HS-2) is a committed entry.

clauses.section: E.2b Replicated D and admitter failover (HC-18 to HC-20)
clauses.text: - **HC-19 Term fence in D.** A host that won `elect(t)` folds the log it received (HS-4 verification of the whole chain, then HC-8), then appends `host.Term` {leader, term} and makes it durable before admitting any input. `t` must exceed every term already in D. Every `host.Window` carries the term. The new admitter's adapters are fresh, so it appends `host.Restarted` after `host.Term` (HC-22), and a request emitted under an older term with no result in D gets one result, `failed` with `interrupted` (HC-3). clauses.section: E.2b Replicated D and admitter failover (HC-18 to HC-20)
clauses.text: - **HC-18a Transport.** Replication follows Raft's AppendEntries and RequestVote: an append carries (prev_idx, prev_term) and a follower does not accept it unless its log has an entry at prev_idx with that term (log matching), deletes a conflicting suffix and appends what is missing. The current term and the vote are written to stable storage before a candidate asks for votes, before a vote is granted, and before an append is acknowledged. A vote goes only to a candidate whose log is at least as up-to-date by (last term, last index). The leader advances the commit index only over entries of it

clauses.section: E.2b Replicated D and admitter failover (HC-18 to HC-20)
clauses.text: - **HC-20 Deposed admitter.** An admitter whose barrier is not granted because a higher term was granted has had its role taken. By HS-3 it appends nothing further and acks nothing, so its unacked inputs are retransmitted to the new admitter and HC-16 removes those that did commit. Committed entries are never removed: the new admitter's log contains every entry a quorum had accepted, so D after a failover extends D before it.

clauses.section: E.4 Inputs are events (HC-10, HC-10a, HC-10b)
clauses.text: **HC-10.** Every value that enters a run is an event or a logged answer in D. This includes key, pointer, resize and focus input; `Tick` and `host.WallTime`; every file, network, PTY, audio and GPU readback result; foreign results and traps; `select nondet` choices; Delivered, TimedOut and Unreachable; capability minting; lifecycle (suspend, resume, process kill); random bytes; and the host entries of E.5. An input that is not in D does not exist for the program.

clauses.section: E.11 Proposed rules (not normative)
clauses.text: - **TU-1 (proposed).** Every primitive value is an n-dimensional tensor `Tensor[elem, shape]`, where `elem` is one of the primitive element types of 5.1 and `shape` is a list of non-negative dimensions. A scalar is the rank 0 tensor `Tensor[elem, []]`. Relation: generalizes the primitive types of 5.1; a version 0.5 to 0.8 program keeps its meaning because each of its scalars is read as rank 0.

clauses.text: - **TU-2 (proposed).** The shape is part of the type and is checked statically. An operation whose operand shapes do not agree (for example a matrix product of `[m, k]` and `[j, n]` with k not equal to j) is a checker error, never a run-time trap. Dimensions are literals or names bound in the signature; a shape that cannot be determined statically requires change. Relation: a new W-rule in 9 when adopted.

clauses.section: E.11 Proposed rules (not normative)
clauses.text: - **TU-3 (proposed).** A record whose fields all have one element type and one shape may be read as a tensor over a named axis (`{x: f64, y: f64}` as `Tensor[f64, [axis: {x, y}]]`). Field names index that axis. A record with mixed field types stays a record.

clauses.section: E.11 Proposed rules (not normative)
clauses.text: - **TU-4 (proposed).** Every reduction over an axis follows N-9: a left fold over the axis in index order unless the program names a different fixed tree. The shape and the named tree, never the thread count or fabric, determine the bits.

clauses.section: E.11 Proposed rules (not normative)
clauses.text: - **TU-5 (proposed).** Text, maps, graphs and sum types remain separate canonical values. They are ragged and are never padded or densified into tensors; a tensor element is never one of them.

clauses.section: E.11 Proposed rules (not normative)
clauses.text: - **TU-6 (proposed).** Placement (HC-12) keys the fabric cost table by (pure operation, element type, shape). Choosing a fabric changes cost only; HC-7 and N-9 fix the result bits.
